precepts.point: Laban said unto Jacob, Surely thou art my bone and my flesh. In the scriptures that phrase means we are family; Jacob abode with him a month, and Laban, because Jacob was his brother, asked what his wages should be.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem “unto his mother’s brethren” and pleaded with “all the family of the house of his mother’s father” to have him reign over them instead of the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal. His closing argument was kinship: “remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.”

That is the same phrase Laban used to Jacob: “Surely thou art my bone and my flesh.” In the scriptures it declares, we are family. Laban is owning Jacob as kin, and it is because Jacob was his brother that he would not have him serve for nought, but asked what his wages should be.

precepts.why: “Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon”: the two names are the same man. So Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal is the son of Gideon, the judge who delivered Israel from Midian, and “the sons of Jerubbaal, which are threescore and ten persons” are Gideon's seventy sons.

precepts.text: Midian was subdued and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon; Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten, for he had many wives, and his concubine that was in Shechem also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech.
precepts.point: Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

note.label: Judges 9: Abimelech and the Fire Out of the Bramble

precepts.why:
Chapter 8 gives the background. “Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon.” Then, “Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten: for he had many wives. And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech.”

That is who Abimelech is: the son of the concubine in Shechem, not of the wives. That is why he goes to Shechem, “unto his mother’s brethren”, his uncles on his mother's side, and has them ask the men of Shechem whether all seventy sons should reign or one. And it is why he says, “remember also that I am your bone and your flesh.” He reminded them he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

precepts.text: The sanctified ones are the prophets and the mighty ones are the angels; the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle, so the Most High himself is in the midst of the armies stirring up war among the kingdoms of nations.
precepts.point: The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.

note.label: Judges 9: Abimelech and the Fire Out of the Bramble

precepts.why:
Read verse 23 carefully: “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem.” The Lord sent it. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things.

Isaiah shows him doing it among the nations: “I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness.” The sanctified ones are the prophets and the mighty ones are the angels. Then, “The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle.”

War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High himself is in the midst of the armies, mustering the host, the armies above and below, stirring up war among the kingdoms of nations. And he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another, as he did between Abimelech and Shechem.

The Most High forms the light and creates darkness, makes peace and creates evil. So an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem is no accident and no work of some other power; “I the Lord do all these things.” He is the one who sent it, so that the blood of the seventy sons of Jerubbaal would come back on the man who slew them and the men who aided him.

“The Lord is a man of war: the Lord is his name. Pharaoh’s chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea.”

Many who think they know God have no idea who they are dealing with. He is a man of war; that is his name. He cast Pharaoh's chariots and captains into the sea, and he sends an evil spirit between a king and the city that made him king. The strife at Shechem is the Lord at war against Abimelech for the blood of his brethren.

Josiah put himself in the midst of a war the Most High had sent Pharaoh to fight, and it cost him his life. The Most High is the one mustering these wars, and he was the one who sent the evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem. When he stirs a war, he is in the midst of it.

And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.” Then Micaiah told the king, “Now therefore, behold, the Lord hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the Lord hath spoken evil concerning thee.”

The Lord put a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab's prophets, that he should go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead. He put an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, that the cruelty done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come back on him and on those who aided him. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.

precepts.text: Sisera the captain fled from the battle and died by the hand of a woman when Jael smote the nail into his temples.
precepts.point: He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

note.label: Judges 9: Abimelech and the Fire Out of the Bramble

precepts.why:
Abimelech begs his armourbearer, “Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him.” It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, and it had happened earlier in this book. Sisera the captain fled from the battle, and “Jael Heber’s wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died.”

Sisera died by the hand of a woman with a nail; Abimelech had his skull crushed by a woman with a millstone, and could only try to hide it by having a young man thrust him through.

Abimelech exalted himself and took the throne as if he had earned it, but he came not in truth, and his heart was full of deceit. God discovered the secret that he had slain his brothers and cast him down in the midst of the congregation: a piece of a millstone on his head at Thebez, his skull broken, dying by his own armourbearer's sword. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit.

note.label: Blood Toucheth Blood

points: Abimelech reigned three years over Israel, and then God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, and they dealt treacherously with him. The Lord flipped the switch on them.

That is the warning: choose your friends carefully. When you pair up with somebody in evil, talking about brothers, sisters and leadership, and everything is good between you, you are marking yourself; the Lord will have you at each other's throats down the line.

points: They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him.

Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal.
With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.
